title: Frosting vs Icing vs Glaze: What's the Difference?
summaryShort: Frosting is thick and fluffy, icing is thinner and sets firm, and glaze is the thinnest and sets into a shiny, sheer coat. In the US the words overlap, and in the UK "icing" often covers all three.
metaTitle: Frosting vs Icing vs Glaze | Incr-EdibleCupCakes
metaDescription: Frosting vs icing vs glaze explained: textures, US and UK terms, glaze ratios and what to use on cupcakes. Read the guide and pick the right topping.
sidebarBullets: Frosting: thick, fluffy, holds a swirl.
Icing: thinner, spreads and sets firm.
Glaze: pourable, sets thin and shiny.
Basic glaze: 1 cup powdered sugar + 1 to 2 Tbsp liquid.
UK "icing" can mean any of the three.

sections.heading: What Is the Difference Between Frosting, Icing and Glaze?
paragraphs: The difference is thickness. Frosting is thick and fluffy, icing is thinner and smooth, and glaze is thin enough to pour.
In my kitchen, I think of them as a scale. Fluffy swirl on one end, sheer shiny coat on the other, and icing sitting in the middle.
list: Frosting: butter or cream cheese based, holds peaks.
Icing: powdered sugar and liquid, spreads and sets.
Glaze: powdered sugar and a lot of liquid, drips and sets thin.

sections.heading: How US and UK Usage Differ
paragraphs: In the US, bakers split the words by texture. In the UK, "icing" is the everyday word for nearly every sweet topping.
A British recipe that says "buttercream icing" means what Americans call buttercream frosting. If a UK recipe says "glacé icing," it means a simple glaze of powdered sugar and water.
list: US: frosting for fluffy toppings, icing for thinner ones.
UK: icing for almost everything, including buttercream.
Read the ingredients and texture, not just the name.

sections.heading: Frosting: Thick, Fluffy and Pipeable
paragraphs: Frosting is the right pick when you want a tall swirl. It is made from fat, such as butter or cream cheese, beaten with powdered sugar until it holds its shape.
The fat is why it stays soft and creamy instead of setting hard. It also means frosting needs cool storage, so check my hot weather guide if your kitchen runs warm.

sections.heading: Icing: Thinner and Sets Firm
paragraphs: Icing is a thinner mix that spreads smoothly and then dries to a soft or firm finish. Most icings are powdered sugar plus milk, water, or sometimes egg white.
It suits flat-topped cupcakes, where a tall swirl would look out of place. Spread it with the back of a spoon while it is still loose, because it starts to crust within minutes.

sections.heading: Glaze: Pourable and Shiny
paragraphs: Glaze is the thinnest of the three and sets into a sheer, glossy layer. A basic glaze is 1 cup powdered sugar mixed with 1 to 2 Tbsp milk or lemon juice.
Start with 1 Tbsp and add liquid a few drops at a time. Too runny, and it soaks into the crumb and disappears. Too thick, and it will not drip nicely off the spoon.
list: Thick glaze: 1 cup sugar + 1 Tbsp liquid, for a bold white coat.
Medium glaze: 1 cup sugar + 1.5 Tbsp liquid, for a classic drizzle.
Thin glaze: 1 cup sugar + 2 Tbsp liquid, for a see-through shine.

sections.heading: Royal Icing for Decorations
paragraphs: Royal icing is a special icing that dries rock hard, so it is best for decorations rather than a cupcake topping. It is made with powdered sugar, pasteurized egg whites or meringue powder, and a little water.

Pipe flowers, sprinkles shapes, or lettering onto parchment and let them dry for several hours. Then set them on top of frosted cupcakes. Keep unused icing covered with a damp cloth, since it crusts fast.

sections.heading: Which One to Use on Cupcakes
paragraphs: Use frosting for swirls, icing for flat tops, and glaze for dense or fruity cupcakes. Match the topping to the crumb: light cakes can handle fluffy frosting, while dense ones like lemon or spice shine with a glaze.
Think about transport too. Glaze and icing travel well, while soft frosting can smudge in a box.

howToSteps: Decide the look you want: tall swirl, smooth flat top, or shiny drizzle.
Pick frosting for a swirl, icing for a flat top, or glaze for a drizzle.
For glaze, stir 1 cup powdered sugar with 1 Tbsp liquid.
Add more liquid a few drops at a time until it runs off the spoon in a ribbon.
Cool the cupcakes fully before topping, or the glaze and icing will melt and slide.
Pour or spread, then let glaze or icing set for 15 to 20 minutes.
Add royal icing decorations once the base topping is set.

faq.question: Is icing the same as frosting?
faq.answer: Not exactly in the US, where frosting is thicker and fluffier than icing. In the UK, people often use the word icing for both.

faq.question: Can I turn frosting into glaze?
faq.answer: Not well. Buttercream has too much fat to thin into a clean glaze. Mix powdered sugar and liquid instead, which takes about two minutes.

faq.question: Why is my glaze see-through and soaking in?
faq.answer: It has too much liquid, or the cupcakes were still warm. Add a spoonful of powdered sugar and cool the cupcakes completely first.

faq.question: How long does royal icing take to dry?
faq.answer: Small decorations dry in about 2 to 4 hours at room temperature. Thicker pieces may need overnight.

faq.question: Does glaze need to be refrigerated?
faq.answer: A plain powdered sugar glaze does not. Glaze made with cream cheese or fresh dairy should be chilled.
